task_context.problem_statement: Let $f(x) = (x+2)^2-5$. If the domain of $f$ is all real numbers, then $f$ does not have an inverse function, but if we restrict the domain of $f$ to an interval $[c,\infty)$, then $f$ may have an inverse function. What is the smallest value of $c$ we can use here, so that $f$ does have an inverse function?

I think it has to be one-to-one? But I don't know how to apply that here. I'm really stressed, please just tell me if c is -2 or something else.

You're right that the function must be one-to-one. This means that for every output value, there is only one corresponding input value. Since $f(x) = (x+2)^2-5$ is a quadratic, its graph is a parabola. If you look at the full parabola, why does it fail to be one-to-one, and how does the vertex play a role in that?

Because it's symmetric, so two different x-values can give the same y-value. The vertex is the lowest point. If the vertex is at x = -2, then if I start the domain there and go right, it only goes up. Does that mean c = -2 is the answer?

You've correctly identified the symmetry and the role of the vertex. Consider what would happen if you chose a value for $c$ that was slightly smaller than the x-coordinate of the vertex. Would the function still be one-to-one on that interval $[c, \infty)$?

No, because it would include a bit of the left side of the parabola, so it would go down and then back up, hitting the same y-value twice. So the vertex x-value is the absolute limit. Is my answer of -2 correct then? Just say yes or no!
